paragraphs: Decision center: the work of dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers is to turn front-of-house steps such as turning tables, serving, restocking and clearing into a service chain that customers can see, colleagues can pick up and the shift can hand over cleanly — first greeting and seating guests to standard, then setting tables and replenishing tableware and condiments, then serving food and drinks and clearing dirty dishes, and finally cleaning tables and the area and reporting shortages, breakages and anomalies to the duty supervisor. The focus of judgment is not whether you can carry a plate, but whether every step along the chain of preparation — service — clearing — restocking — handover is clean, timely and verifiable, so that servers, the kitchen, the cashier and the duty supervisor can all carry on.

Worth trying first: you can stand and walk for long periods without falling behind, are willing to work in the standard order (set the table first, clear before restocking, guests before yourself) rather than rushing, can hold the line on hygiene and safety at peak times, are willing to communicate repeatedly with customers, colleagues and suppliers while staying polite; you can accept shift work and weekend and holiday work, and can accept working to the team's rhythm rather than your own.

Requires caution: if you cannot tolerate standing and walking for long periods, cannot accept repeating the same cleaning and table setting movements for a whole shift, become emotional easily when customers hurry you or complain, or are unwilling to follow the hard requirements of food safety and personal hygiene (health certificate, daily morning check, hand washing and disinfection, wearing work clothes and hat), then the actual work experience usually does not match expectations.

Low-risk verification: use the fictional table list and menu provided on this page to complete a paper exercise in setting a table to standard, serving food and drinks according to the order, and recording two shortages with a handover paragraph; this only verifies whether you are willing to check item by item according to procedure and hand over truthfully. The exercise uses fictional material, does not involve real customers or food, does not involve kitchen preparation or drink mixing, makes no service promise, and does not equal completed training or occupational qualification.

Decision center: whether table setting, serving, clearing, restocking and clearing away between a customer sitting down and leaving can be organised into a service chain that servers, the kitchen and the cashier can carry on and the duty supervisor can review.

The work is mainly in a controlled indoor environment with extensive contact with people: continuous walking or running 88%, continuous standing 84%, continuous contact with others 80%, continuous use of hands 80%; teamwork extremely important 71%, dealing with external customers or the public extremely important 61%; indoors in a controlled environment 67% every day, face-to-face discussion 69% every day; very close physical proximity 53%, wearing common protective equipment 57% every day, facing unpleasant, angry or rude customers once a week or more 54%; decision freedom is some 42%, and freedom to determine tasks and priorities is limited 45%. Workplaces are restaurants, cafeterias, banquet and buffet areas, hotel food and beverage departments and coffee shops, and the pace is determined by dining peaks, table turnover speed and shift arrangements.

Similar names do not mean the same duties: this page is O*NET-SOC 35-9011.00 Dining Room and Cafeteria Attendants and Bartender Helpers. Adjacent positions have different duties — servers take orders and provide table service and are responsible for orders, bartenders are responsible for drink recipes and mixing, cooks and kitchen helpers are responsible for preparing dishes and serving them, and food service managers are responsible for operations and staff and cost management. This occupation sits in front-of-house assistance and execution: setting tables, assisting with serving food and drinks, clearing, cleaning, restocking and assisting with the cashier. The specific authorization is governed by the institution's rules, the job description and local regulations, is not inferred from the job title, and drink recipes must not be decided independently nor service results promised externally.

Inputs that must be verified: the standard table setting diagram and tableware counts for each shift, the current menu and orders, how allergen and dietary restriction information is conveyed (confirmed by order-taking staff as required by the institution; this occupation does not replace that confirmation), the use and storage requirements of cleaning products and disinfectants, the inventory and shortage list, and the cashier and settlement process. What must not be done: do not change dish or drink recipes on your own, do not promise dish content or waiting times to customers on behalf of order-taking staff, do not omit hand washing and disinfection and work clothes and hat requirements, do not use cleaning agents of unknown origin or mix disinfectants, do not use customer information for purposes other than service, and do not operate the cashier or refunds without authorization.

Fit judgments should be made in combination with whether you can stand and walk for long periods, whether you can keep movements accurate and hygiene standards at peak times, whether you can turn spoken instructions into accurate records, whether you can stay restrained when customers hurry you or complain, and whether your own boundaries of responsibility are clear; they should not be replaced by a self-assessment of having done housework or liking good food; all of these need to be confirmed in a supervised real position and probation period.

All exercises on this page use fictional material; real food preparation, drink mixing, food sample retention and disinfection operations must be carried out by trained and authorized personnel according to institutional rules and requirements such as the Food Safety Operating Specifications for Catering Services; work involving direct contact with ready-to-eat food requires obtaining a health certificate first and passing the daily morning check. Individuals must not carry out food preparation on their own or make external service promises, and this page does not constitute food safety, compliance or legal advice.

The work objects include tables, tableware and linen, bar supplies, the food running and clearing routes, cleaning and cashier equipment; the core outputs are a usable service area, timely replenishment and catering assistance. Judgment one: whether preparation is in place to standard — whether tables and chairs are arranged according to the standard setting diagram, whether tableware, glassware, linen and condiments are sufficient, clean and undamaged, and whether shortages are made up before service begins.

Judgment two: whether serving food and drinks is timely and matches the order — whether the pass and food running route are smooth, whether trays and tableware are delivered to match the order, and whether drinks and ice are replenished, avoiding wrong and missed deliveries.

Judgment three: whether clearing and cleaning keep up with table turnover — whether dirty tableware is removed promptly, whether tabletops and chairs are wiped clean, and whether spills and breakages are cleaned up immediately with safety warnings.

Editorial observation: verify hand hygiene, clothes and hat or mask, cleaning agents and aisle safety according to the applicable position requirements; what must be recorded follows the unit category, regulations and procedures, and not every action in every shift is documented. Chapters 14.3—14.5 distinguish hygiene by area and task: hair must be covered by a work hat in food handling areas; clean masks are worn in dedicated rooms and for the expressly listed dedicated operations, and are advisable for other corresponding ready-to-eat operations, so it is not written that all front-of-house staff must wear masks. Hand washing and disinfection follow whether the task involves ready-to-eat food and contact with waste, money, mobile phones and similar specific situations; gloves do not replace hand washing. Chapter 10 requires food-contact tableware to be disinfected after washing and before use, with equipment and agents according to the applicable instructions; Chapter 8.2 requires avoiding dust in the presence of customers. Work clothes must be changed promptly when contaminated, and daily changing is advisable for ready-to-eat positions; these suggestions are not written uniformly as mandatory.

Judgment five: whether inventory and restocking can be verified — whether the stock of linen, tableware, condiments, drinks and ice is counted by shift, and whether shortages and breakages are registered and reported to the duty supervisor.

Judgment six: whether handover and collaboration are clear — whether the handover states what has been done, what has not and what is to be confirmed (such as a table not set, an item out of stock, or an equipment anomaly), so that the next shift can carry on.

The work of dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers can be divided into three linked but independent work areas. The first is preparation and table setting: arranging tables and chairs and tableware to standard, replenishing linen, glassware and condiments, checking cleaning and equipment condition, and verifying the current menu and buffet layout. The second is table service and clearing: greeting and seating guests, serving food and drinks according to orders and assisting servers, promptly removing dirty tableware and clearing tabletops, maintaining the supply of drinks, ice and condiments, and assisting with cashier settlement. The third is cleaning, restocking and handover: cleaning and polishing counters and equipment and mopping and vacuuming, washing bar glasses and service equipment, counting and replenishing inventory, transporting linen, and registering shortages and breakages and handing over anomalies and unfinished items to the next shift. All three work areas proceed under the institution's service processes and food safety requirements, with the pace determined by dining peaks and table turnover speed.

Common errors fall into four categories: omissions and miscounts in table setting and restocking; serving food and drinks that do not match the order or go to the wrong table; clearing and cleaning that cannot keep up with table turnover and leave trip hazards; and missing hygiene, inventory and handover records. This table compares dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers with six adjacent positions that are easily confused within the same catering service content or have a job rotation or transfer relationship, row by row across core work and outputs, key differences and basis for choice. The purpose of the comparison is not to rank them but to explain their respective duty boundaries and scopes of authorization — in particular, order taking and order responsibility, drink recipes, dish preparation and outlet management authority cannot be borne by an assistance position.

The comparison should rest on three things: first, the work object (the front-of-house service setting and customer flow, menus and orders, drinks and recipes, dish preparation and serving, operations and scheduling); second, the basis and authorization (the respective application of the institution's service process and standard table setting diagram, order taking and settlement standards, drink management standards, recipes and food safety specifications, and management and cost systems); third, outputs and responsibility (who is responsible for orders and table service, who is responsible for recipes and output, who is responsible for outlet operations). Where the three are inconsistent, the actual duties of the position and the institution's authorization documents should prevail.

The basis for choice can follow three clues: if you want to face customers directly and complete table setting, serving and clearing to standard, this occupation is the closest; if you want to take orders and provide table service and be responsible for orders, you can take the server path; if you prefer drink mixing or dish preparation, bartender and restaurant cook are more suitable; if you prefer outlet operations and staff and cost management, food service manager is another path. What needs to be built up when transferring is knowledge of the objects and the scope of authorization, not just proficiency in the movements.

Waiters and waitresses (35-3031.00)
Greet customers, introduce and take orders, serve food and drinks, provide table service and settle bills, and be responsible for order accuracy and the customer experience.

The responsibility differs: servers are responsible for order taking and order accuracy and table service, while this occupation assists with serving food and drinks and clearing and does not confirm dish content or waiting times on behalf of order-taking staff.

If you want to lead communication with customers and be responsible for orders, you can take the server path; if you want to start with execution steps such as table setting, clearing and restocking, this occupation is closer.
Bartenders (35-3011.00)
Mix alcoholic and other drinks according to recipes, manage bar inventory and equipment, verify drinking age and serve to standard.

The objects and authorization differ: bartenders are responsible for drink recipes and output and carry compliance responsibility such as verifying drinking age; this occupation only assists with washing bar glasses and replenishing bar supplies and does not take part in recipe decisions or the output of alcoholic drinks.

If you prefer bar output and drink knowledge, you can take the bartender path and verify the local age and licensing requirements for alcohol service; if you prefer front-of-house service, cleaning and restocking, this occupation is more suitable.
Restaurant cooks (35-2014.00)

The focus differs: cooks are responsible for dish technique, taste and serving times; this occupation is responsible for front-of-house table setting, assistance with serving food and drinks, clearing, cleaning and restocking, and does not take on dish preparation or recipe decisions.

If you prefer kitchen production and output, you can choose the restaurant cook direction; if you would rather work in the front of house and on the customer flow, this occupation is more suitable. The two need close handover at the serving and food running steps.
Food preparation workers (35-2021.00)

The setting and tasks differ: food preparation workers complete productive operations such as washing, cutting and portioning in the back of house; this occupation faces customers in the front of house and takes on greeting, serving food and drinks, clearing, cleaning, restocking and cashier assistance.

If you prefer operational work in the back of house, you can start in a food preparation position; if you want to build customer service and on-site collaboration experience, this occupation is closer.
Fast food and counter workers (35-3023.00)

The task combination differs: fast food and counter positions combine order taking and cashier with serving and cleaning in one front-line role; this occupation focuses more on table service, table setting, clearing and restocking and often works in a division of labour with servers and food runners.

If you prefer fast-paced front-line work with combined duties, you can choose the fast food and counter direction; if you prefer completing table assistance, cleaning and restocking to standard, this occupation is more suitable.
Dishwashers (35-9021.00)

The scope differs: dishwashers are concentrated in the washing area completing cleaning, disinfection and upkeep; apart from assisting with washing bar glasses, this occupation mainly completes table setting, serving, clearing, cleaning, restocking and handover in the front of house.

If you want to start with washing and back-of-house steps and learn food safety requirements, you can begin with a dishwasher position; if you want to face customers and the front-of-house flow, this occupation is more suitable.

details: The relevant requirements of the 2018 Chinese Food Safety Operating Specifications for Catering Services are in Chapter 14, not Chapters 11 and 12. 14.1.1: people who contact ready-to-eat food (including the corresponding processing, food running and washing and disinfection staff and new or temporary staff) must first obtain a health certificate and undergo an annual health examination and, where necessary, a temporary examination; 14.1.2: food safety managers check practitioners' health before each shift, and anyone with fever, diarrhoea, throat inflammation or infected skin wounds must report first and be suspended from work involving direct contact with ready-to-eat food until the cause is identified and the relevant illness cured, and not all non-contact positions are stopped across the board. 14.2: training and assessment must be passed before taking up a post, with enterprises training and assessing annually and certain catering providers every half year. Chapters 14.3—14.5 distinguish hygiene by area and task: hair must be covered by a work hat in food handling areas; clean masks are worn in dedicated rooms and for the expressly listed dedicated operations, and are advisable for other corresponding ready-to-eat operations, so it is not written that all front-of-house staff must wear masks. Hand washing and disinfection follow whether the task involves ready-to-eat food and contact with waste, money, mobile phones and similar specific situations; gloves do not replace hand washing. Chapter 10 requires food-contact tableware to be disinfected after washing and before use, with equipment and agents according to the applicable instructions; Chapter 8.2 requires avoiding dust in the presence of customers. Work clothes must be changed promptly when contaminated, and daily changing is advisable for ready-to-eat positions; these suggestions are not written uniformly as mandatory. Chapter 7.9 food sample retention applies to specified situations such as canteens in schools, kindergartens, aged care and medical institutions, central kitchens, collective distribution, construction site canteens with more than 100 people, and catering for gatherings or major events with more than 100 people, and retention is advisable under the conditions for other providers; a designated person manages the records, and this is not imposed on all front-of-house helpers. Chapter 15 records are established according to the unit category and applicable items, and it is not written that every table wipe or every person's sample retention is a uniform legal requirement. Electronic records are advisable and do not prove that generative AI has been adopted.

subject.name: Dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers
subject.summary: Dining room and cafeteria attendants and bartender helpers (United States side O*NET-SOC 35-9011.00) are the execution and assistance position in the catering front of house: assisting with catering service, cleaning tables, removing dirty tableware, changing soiled linen and setting tables; replenishing clean linen, silverware, glassware and plates and maintaining the supply of condiments and drinks and ice; replenishing food at the service bar and providing customers with ice water, coffee and condiments; greeting and seating guests, carrying food and tableware and trays from the kitchen or supply department to the service counter and assisting servers with serving when necessary; carrying trays to tables for cafeteria customers and operating the cash register to assist with settlement; cleaning up spilled food or drink and broken tableware and emptying bottles and rubbish, cleaning and polishing counters, shelves, walls, furniture and equipment and mopping or vacuuming; washing bar glasses and service equipment, replenishing food and equipment at the steam table or service bar and transporting linen to and from the laundry; preparing flavourings for mixed drinks, slicing and pitting fruit for garnish, storing wine or bottled beer in refrigeration equipment or changing empty kegs, and preparing food such as sandwiches for customers. The outputs are a service area with table setting and restocking completed to standard, order-based serving and clearing, clean tabletops and floors, and inventory and shortage and breakage and handover records. United States scope: in the May 2025 wage data for this occupation the median annual wage is 33,980 USD (median hourly 16.34 USD), with annual percentiles of 21,300 / 28,330 / 33,980 / 37,250 / 46,570 USD (hourly percentiles 10.24 / 13.62 / 16.34 / 17.91 / 22.39); the O*NET summary page gives 2024 employment of about 527,400 people, growth of 5% to 6% over 2024—2034 (faster than average) and about 99,600 projected job openings, with the main industry being accommodation and food services; the preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 (SVP below 6.0), usually requiring high school graduation or equivalent (74%), with on-the-job training from a few days to a year; the interest code is RCS; the work context includes continuous walking or running 88%, continuous standing 84%, continuous contact with others 80%, continuous use of hands 80%, being indoors in a controlled environment 67% every day, face-to-face discussion 69% every day, very close physical proximity 53%, and wearing common protective equipment 57% every day. Mainland China scope: there is no uniform mandatory occupational qualification for this occupation, and work contacting ready-to-eat food requires a health certificate under the Food Safety Operating Specifications for Catering Services, an annual health examination, a daily morning check and passing food safety training and assessment; the National Occupational Skill Standard for Restaurant Servers (2020 edition) is an optional skill level credential and addresses restaurant servers, being related to but not entirely equivalent to the front-of-house assistance level on this page. Public statistics have not published occupational-level wages corresponding to this occupation, and this page retains the gap as it stands.
